candidates.attacker_control: The names of authorization resources, policies (including permissions) and scopes are free-form strings supplied through the administrative REST API (e.g. .../authz/resource-server/resource|policy|scope create/update) and returned verbatim in JSON responses that populate the AngularJS $scope objects used by authz-controller.js. An actor with the ability to manage authorization settings for a client (e.g. a delegated client/realm admin, or any principal able to create/rename such entities) controls these strings, including characters such as '<', '>' and event-handler text.
candidates.counterevidence_checked:
Checked whether the generic Dialog service is also affected: themes/.../js/services.js openDialog sets $scope.message plainly and templates/kc-modal.html renders {{message}}, so Angular escapes that path — only the authz dialog uses $sce.trustAsHtml plus ng-bind-html. Checked whether the message contains intended markup: yes (

/

    /
  • are intentional formatting), so the defect is not the trusted-HTML pattern per se but the unescaped interpolation of attacker-controlled names into it; escaped alternatives exist in sibling code (escapeHtml used for 'type' in services.js:46/1935). Checked the default CSP (ContentSecurityPolicyBuilder) — no script-src restriction, so XSS is not blocked; X-XSS-Protection is legacy and not relied upon. Considered that creating the malicious name may require delegated administrative rights (a precondition, not a blocker for the XSS). Considered that this could be the pre-fix state of an admin-console XSS fixed shortly after 20.0.1, but no patch/CVE data was inspected or available. Verified there are no other Keycloak-authored ng-bind-html/trustAsHtml sinks in the themes tree (only this authz modal).
candidates.impact: Script execution in the Keycloak admin console origin under the victim administrator's authenticated session. Practical consequences include access to admin-console tokens/session material, performing administrative REST calls as the victim (including actions the attacker could not perform directly), and privilege escalation from a narrowly delegated authorization/client manager to broader realm control, plus data modification/exfiltration. This is the classic stored-XSS-in-admin-UI escalation pattern; no credential theft beyond the browser session is required.
candidates.prerequisites: A principal able to create or rename an authorization resource/policy/scope for a client whose resource server pages are visible in the admin console; a victim with admin-console access who opens the client's Authorization pages and triggers the delete confirmation for the crafted entity (the vulnerable dialog is invoked from the resource/policy/scope list and detail delete actions); the admin console is the AngularJS theme shipped in this snapshot, and the default Content-Security-Policy (ContentSecurityPolicyBuilder default: frame-src/frame-ancestors/object-src only) does not include script-src, so injected inline/JS markup is not blocked. Legacy X-XSS-Protection does not mitigate modern browsers.
candidates.root_cause: The admin-console authorization dialogs build their confirmation text by string-concatenating entity names returned by the server ($scope.resource.name, $scope.policy.name, $scope.scope.name, permissions[i].name, dependentPolicies[i].name) without HTML escaping (authz-services.js:112-114 and 129-131; authz-controller.js:89-101, 116-131, 450-468), and the resulting string is explicitly marked as trusted HTML via $sce.trustAsHtml(message) (authz-services.js:82-84) and rendered with ng-bind-html="message" (templates/authz/kc-authz-modal.html:7). $sce.trustAsHtml bypasses Angular's contextual escaping/sanitization, so markup placed in a name becomes live DOM/JS in the admin console origin.
candidates.title: Stored XSS in Keycloak admin console authorization dialogs via unescaped resource/policy/scope names rendered as trusted HTML
candidates.trace:
1) Names are stored/served by the authorization REST API and loaded into $scope.resource/$scope.policy/$scope.scope (authz-controller.js). 2) On delete, Resources.delete/Policies.delete/Scopes.delete concatenate these names into msg, e.g. msg += "
  • " + permissions[i].name + "
    • " (authz-controller.js:94-95, 124-125) and AuthzDialog.confirmDeleteWithMsg($scope.resource.name, ...) (authz-controller.js:101, 131, 468). 3) AuthzDialog.confirmDeleteWithMsg/confirmDelete concatenates name into the dialog message without escaping: "... " + name + " ?" (authz-services.js:114, 131). 4) openDialog's controller executes $scope.message = $sce.trustAsHtml(message) (authz-services.js:84), marking the whole string, including attacker markup, as safe HTML. 5) The authz modal template renders it with
    (kc-authz-modal.html:7), inserting the markup into the DOM in the admin-console origin. Because the value is trusted, ng-bind-html performs no sanitization, so an injected element/event handler executes when the dialog is shown.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed: no code, tests, or exploit payloads were executed. I could not verify the exact permission level an attacker needs to set authorization entity names in a given realm, whether any deployment-level sanitization/filter applies to authz names, or which CVE/ground-truth anomaly this snapshot corresponds to. The snapshot contains no .ftl view templates, so template-based XSS could not be assessed; the relation index provides only syntactic navigation, not data flow.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-79 Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting') — stored XSS in privileged UI

coverage_summary: Tool-reported scope: 5,889 source files (4,704 Java) were visible; get_source_scope reports no exclusions for binaries, symlinks, sensitive names, or size (0 over 5 MiB). get_relation_scope reports a partial, syntax-only index: 5,798 indexed files, 91 source files missing from the index, 94 omitted files, 61,860 symbols / 143,214 calls / 130,069 edges with 87,825 unresolved calls, and explicitly no control-flow, data-flow, semantic resolution, or runtime/Spring enforcement analysis; 0 index build errors reported but build_or_tests_run=false. I inspected (read directly or via targeted literal searches) the main OIDC endpoints (AuthorizationEndpointChecker, LogoutEndpoint, TokenEndpoint, PKCE utilities, PAR/device/CIBA area, redirect utilities), SAML core/broker/service signature and issuer/InResponseTo handling, X.509 certificate lookup and authenticator implementations, theme and resource loading/encoding helpers, selected admin REST/authorization and client-policy code, the Keycloak-authored admin/account console JS/HTML, and grep sweeps for classic sink patterns (process execution, deserialization, SQL construction, path handling, redirects, trusted-HTML sinks, weak crypto/TLS). The relation index was used only for navigation and each traced edge/location was verified against source text. The snapshot does not contain .ftl templates, so template-level rendering paths (login/account/admin views) could not be reviewed; most of the repository (adapters, model providers, operator, migration, and the very large testsuite) was covered only by targeted search rather than exhaustive reading.
limitations: No code, tests, scanners, or exploit payloads were executed; the candidate is a source-evidence lead, not a runtime-confirmed vulnerability.

The P1 relation index is syntactic only (no data-flow/control-flow/semantic resolution) and omits 91 source files plus 94 omitted files; absence of an index record for an area does not mean it was reviewed.
No .ftl template files exist in the assigned snapshot, so Freemarker-based XSS/rendering issues in login, account, and admin pages could not be assessed.
Exact permission requirements (who may create/rename authorization resources/policies/scopes) and deployment-specific sanitization/CSP overrides could not be verified from source.

I did not inspect or use any ground-truth labels, patches, CVE/CWE mappings, or other runs; consequently the mapping between this snapshot and any specific CVE/ground-truth location remains uncertain, and other vulnerabilities may exist in uninspected areas.

The admin-console theme files present in the snapshot are the AngularJS admin console; if a deployment serves a different theme or disables this console, the selected candidate would not apply as described.

rejected_leads.lead: Open redirect via realm-wide logout redirect validation: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/protocol/oidc/endpoints/LogoutEndpoint.java:243-255 falls back to RedirectUtils.verifyRealmRedirectUri (RedirectUtils.java:44-53), i.e. it validates a user-supplied post-logout/redirect URI against all enabled clients' resolved redirect URIs when the client cannot be determined from id_token_hint/client_id.
rejected_leads.reason: Real weakness pattern (CWE-601), but exploitation requires either a registered client whose redirect URIs are permissive/wildcard (so an attacker-chosen absolute URI can match), the deprecated legacy logout redirect switch enabled, or an ID token for a client that no longer exists; the code comment shows the fallback is intentional compatibility behavior, and I could not demonstrate attacker control of a matching registered URI from source alone. Kept as an unconfirmed lead, not the selected candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: X.509 client authentication weaknesses: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authentication/authenticators/client/X509ClientAuthenticator.java:131-149 matches the client's configured subject DN against every certificate in the presented chain (not only the leaf), and services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/protocol/oidc/OIDCAdvancedConfigWrapper.java:218-222 enables regex interpretation of the literal subject DN by default when the attribute is absent (the admin UI appears to default the checkbox to off).
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible client-impersonation/authentication-bypass conditions (the code asymmetry with the UI default is suspicious), but exploitability depends on mTLS deployment details I cannot verify from source (truststore contents/issuance of a chain certificate whose subject DN matches the target client's configured DN, TLS termination behavior). Left as an unconfirmed lead; the selected candidate has a complete, verifiable source-to-sink chain.

rejected_leads.lead: services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/encoding/GzipResourceEncodingProvider.java:41 checks encodedFile.getCanonicalPath().startsWith(cacheDir.getCanonicalPath()) without a trailing File.separator, so a sibling path sharing the cache-dir prefix could pass the check.
rejected_leads.reason: File path components are constrained upstream (theme names and resource paths pass canonical-path guards in FolderTheme/FolderThemeProvider) and the write requires a real theme resource, so a concrete escape/impact could not be established; rejected as a standalone finding.

summary: Reviewed the Keycloak 20.0.1 snapshot (5,889 files; 4,704 Java) as a defensive source assessment. Scope/coverage was established via get_source_scope (no binary/symlink/sensitive-name exclusions; 0 files >5 MiB) and get_relation_scope (index partial: 5,798 indexed files, 91 source files missing, 94 omitted; syntax-only relations; no data-flow/control-flow/semantic resolution; Spring annotation candidates unverified). I traced attacker-controlled input through OIDC endpoints (authorization/logout/token/PAR/device, PKCE, redirect validation), SAML broker/service signature and Issuer/InResponseTo checks, X.509 certificate lookup/authenticator paths, theme/resource loading (FolderTheme/traversal guards), client-policy flows, and the admin/account console front-end code. The single strongest candidate is a stored XSS in the admin console's authorization (authz) delete-confirmation dialogs: resource/policy/scope names obtained from server responses are concatenated into an HTML string that is explicitly marked trusted ($sce.trustAsHtml) and rendered with ng-bind-html, so a crafted entity name executes script in an administrator's session. Two other real-issue areas (logout endpoint realm-wide post_logout_redirect_uri validation, and X.509 client-auth DN/regex matching) were examined but are weaker as the case's target and are listed as rejected/unconfirmed leads. No code was executed and no tests/scanners were run; findings are source-evidence leads, not runtime-confirmed vulnerabilities.
